title: Intoxicants set aside
hookLine: wine and intoxicants are set aside because their harm outweighs their benefit (2:219; 5:90)

lines: WINE IN THE STREETS OF MEDINA.
cards: Picture a town where almost everyone drinks. Wine at dinner, wine at weddings, poems written in its praise, merchants who make their living from it. Now picture that town giving it up.
Not over a generation, with campaigns and fines. In an afternoon. A report in Bukhari says that when the final word came, the companion Anas was pouring drinks at a gathering.
Someone called out the news, and they poured the jars out, until wine ran in the streets of Medina. How does a whole town get there? Slowly, and then all at once.

teach.b: The Arabic word is khamr, usually translated wine or strong drink. Its root means to cover, the same root as khimar, a woman's head covering. The companion Umar explained it in Bukhari: khamr is whatever covers the mind.
The Qur'an didn't forbid it all at once.

First, in Surah al-Baqarah, people ask about strong drink and gambling, and the answer weighs them: there's some benefit in them for people, but, in Pickthall's words, the sin of them is greater than their usefulness.
An honest scale, not a slammed door.
Later, Surah an-Nisa tells believers not to come to prayer while intoxicated.
Finally, Surah al-Ma'idah, verse ninety, calls strong drink, gambling and idols a work of Shaytan, and says: Leave it aside in order that ye may succeed. That's when the jars were poured out.
Aisha, in Bukhari, reflected on the order. If the first verses to come down had said, don't drink wine, people would have said, we will never give it up.
Hearts were prepared first. Rules came later. Muslims take the prohibition as settled.

Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying every intoxicant is khamr, so most scholars apply it to anything that clouds the mind the same way, including drugs, and discuss medical exceptions carefully.
And it's a rule Muslims keep for themselves, not a reason to look down on anyone else at the table. Underneath is the point Umar named. The mind is what you pray with, choose with, and love with.

how: Muslims abstain from alcohol and other intoxicants, following 5:90 and the hadith that every intoxicant is khamr; most scholars extend this to drugs that cloud the mind.

o: a drink shared at a wedding feast
a strong drink allowed in small amounts
anything that covers and clouds the mind

games.q: what's inside khamr — tap the pairs.
p: the sin greater than the use

s: the prohibition came in one verse, all at once
it came in stages: 2:219, then 4:43, then 5:90.
khamr shares a root with khimar, a head covering
both come from a root meaning to cover. Umar: khamr is whatever covers the mind.
the Qur'an says strong drink has no benefit at all
2:219 says there is some benefit, but the sin is greater than the usefulness.

games.q: you're Anas, pouring drinks at a gathering in Medina. someone calls out that the final verse has come down. what happens?
o: they pour the jars out, and wine runs in the streets
they wait to see what others do
games.why: Bukhari reports the jars were poured out until wine ran in the streets of Medina. slowly, and then all at once.

practice: Ask honestly: what covers my mind most days? It may not be a drink at all: the phone at midnight, anger that's been simmering, too little sleep, a feed that leaves you foggy.
Name one without fixing it, and notice how the room feels with a clear head right now; if you pray, you can ask for help with it.

wordCard.voice: Khamr. Wine and anything that covers the mind, set aside in the Qur'an because its harm outweighs its benefit. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: wine, strong drink, from a root meaning to cover.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the mind clear. It took a whole town one afternoon, after years of preparing hearts. Until tomorrow.
